sections.title: Letters, sounds and vowel harmony
sections.summary: Turkish spelling is phonetic and its 29 letters are easy to learn, but every suffix in the language changes shape to match the vowels of the word it joins. This chapter covers the letters, the special sounds ğ and dotless ı, and the two vowel-harmony patterns you will use on every page that follows.

rules.title: The alphabet: 29 letters, one sound each
rules.body: Turkish uses the Latin alphabet with 29 letters. The letters q, w and x are not used; instead there are six extra letters: ç, ğ, ı, ö, ş, ü. Spelling is phonetic: each letter has one sound and every written letter is pronounced, so once you know the letters you can read any word aloud. There are no silent letters and no double-letter tricks.

rules.title: Consonants that differ from English
rules.body: c sounds like English j in 'jam' (cam = glass). ç is ch as in 'chair' (çay = tea). ş is sh as in 'ship' (şehir = city). j is the s of 'measure' and appears only in loanwords (jandarma). y is always a consonant as in 'yes', h is always pronounced (hava), and r is lightly tapped. v is softer than English v, halfway to w.

rules.title: Dotless ı and dotted i
rules.body: Turkish has two letters where English has one. Dotted i sounds like ee in 'see' (bir, iki). Dotless ı is a back vowel, close to the a in 'sofa' or the i in 'cousin' (kız, ılık). The dot survives in capitals: the capital of i is İ and the capital of ı is I, so you write İstanbul and İzmir but Isparta and ILIK. Mixing them up changes words: sık (often) and sik are not the same word.

rules.title: Eight vowels in two groups
rules.body: The vowels are a, e, ı, i, o, ö, u, ü. They split into back vowels (a, ı, o, u) and front vowels (e, i, ö, ü); this split drives vowel harmony. They also split into rounded (o, ö, u, ü) and unrounded (a, e, ı, i). ö is like German ö or French 'eu' (göz), ü like German ü or French 'u' (üzüm). Turkish vowels are short and pure; there are no diphthongs as in English 'go' or 'day'.

rules.title: Two-way harmony: e or a
rules.body: Many suffixes have two forms, one with e and one with a: the plural -ler/-lar, the locative -de/-da, the ablative -den/-dan. To choose, look at the last vowel of the word. After a front vowel (e, i, ö, ü) use the e form; after a back vowel (a, ı, o, u) use the a form. Only the last vowel matters, however many syllables the word has.

rules.title: Four-way harmony: i, ı, u or ü
rules.body: Other suffixes have four forms, such as -im (my), the accusative -i and the question particle mi. After e or i use i; after a or ı use ı; after o or u use u; after ö or ü use ü. In other words the suffix vowel copies the front/back and rounded/unrounded quality of the last vowel. A good test word for any suffix is a set like ev, kız, okul, göz.

rules.title: ğ, the soft g
rules.body: ğ (yumuşak g) is never pronounced like a hard English g. After a back vowel it simply lengthens that vowel: dağ sounds like 'daa', ağaç like 'aaç'. Between front vowels it sounds like a faint y: değil is roughly 'deyil'. It never begins a word, so no Turkish word starts with ğ. In suffixes it appears when a final k softens before a vowel (ekmek, ekmeği).

rules.title: Consonant changes where suffixes join
rules.body: Two sound changes happen at suffix boundaries. First, a suffix beginning with d (-de, -den, -di) turns its d into t after a voiceless consonant (p, ç, t, k, s, ş, h, f): kitapta, sokaktan, Ahmet'te. Second, a final p, ç, t or k usually softens to b, c, d or ğ when a suffix beginning with a vowel is added: kitap but kitabı, ağaç but ağacı, ekmek but ekmeği. Most one-syllable words (at, atı; top, topu) and many loanwords (saat, saati) keep the hard consonant.

examples.en: the horse (object; one syllable, no change)

rules.title: Stress, loanwords and the suffixes that never change
rules.body: Stress usually falls on the last syllable of a word (araBA, kiTAP), though many place names are stressed earlier (ANkara, İsTANbul). Loanwords such as otel, kitap and taksi may mix front and back vowels inside the word, but suffixes always follow the last vowel: otelde, kitaplar. A few suffixes never harmonise at all: -yor (present continuous), -ken (while), -ki (the one that) and -leyin (at the time of).

examples.en: at the hotel (last vowel e, so -de)

sections.title: Nouns, plurals and no gender
sections.summary: Turkish nouns have no gender and no definite article, which removes two of the hardest parts of many European languages. This chapter covers the plural ending -ler/-lar, the little word bir, and the places where English uses a plural but Turkish does not.

rules.title: No grammatical gender
rules.body: Turkish nouns, adjectives and pronouns have no gender. There is no masculine or feminine, and one pronoun o covers he, she and it. Words for people are likewise neutral: arkadaş is a friend of either sex, kardeş a brother or sister, öğretmen a male or female teacher. If you need to specify, you add a word such as kız (girl) or erkek (male): kız kardeş = sister.

examples.en: He is a doctor. / She is a doctor.

rules.title: No word for 'the'
rules.body: Turkish has no definite article. ev means both 'house' and 'the house', and context decides which. When a noun is the direct object of a verb, definiteness is shown instead by the accusative ending -i (Chapter 5): kitap okuyorum = I'm reading a book, kitabı okuyorum = I'm reading the book. Everywhere else, simply leave the noun bare.

rules.title: bir: 'one' and 'a'
rules.body: bir is the number one and also serves as the indefinite article 'a/an'. It is used less than English 'a': a bare noun is often enough (Öğretmenim = I'm a teacher). When an adjective is present, bir normally stands between the adjective and the noun: güzel bir ev = a nice house. Putting bir first (bir güzel ev) is possible but sounds emphatic or literary.

rules.title: The plural -ler / -lar
rules.body: The plural ending is -ler after a front vowel and -lar after a back vowel, following two-way harmony. It attaches directly to the noun. Because it begins with a consonant, the final consonant of the noun never softens: kitaplar, ağaçlar, not kitablar. Pronouns and demonstratives pluralise the same way: onlar (they), bunlar (these).

rules.title: No plural after numbers and quantity words
rules.body: After a number or a word of quantity the noun stays singular: üç elma (three apples), çok kitap (many books), kaç öğrenci? (how many students?), birçok insan (many people), birkaç gün (a few days). The same applies after units of measure: iki kilo elma, bir bardak çay. Adding -ler here is a classic learner mistake and sounds wrong.

rules.title: When the plural is used anyway
rules.body: The plural appears on nouns taken as a general class: Kediler süt sever (cats like milk), Türkler çay sever. A surname or first name with -ler means that person's family or group: Yılmazlar = the Yılmaz family, Ahmetler = Ahmet and his family or friends. The plural is also used in greetings and polite formulas: iyi günler (good day), iyi geceler (good night), teşekkürler (thanks).

rules.title: Adjectives and demonstratives come first and stay singular
rules.body: An adjective stands before its noun and never takes the plural: güzel evler (nice houses), not güzeller evler. The demonstratives bu (this), şu (that, near, pointed at) and o (that, over there) work the same way: bu ev, şu evler, o kitaplar. Used on their own as pronouns they do pluralise: bunlar (these), şunlar (those), onlar (those / they).

rules.title: Bey and Hanım: polite titles after the first name
rules.body: To address or refer to someone politely, add Bey (Mr) or Hanım (Mrs, Ms) after the FIRST name: Ahmet Bey, Ayşe Hanım. Bay and Bayan go before a surname in formal writing (Bay Yılmaz), but in speech Bey and Hanım with the first name are far more common. Job titles also take them: Doktor Bey, Müdür Hanım.

sections.title: Personal endings and 'to be'
sections.summary: Turkish has no verb 'to be' in the present; instead a set of personal endings attaches to nouns and adjectives (öğretmenim = I am a teacher). This chapter covers those endings, the negative değil, the formal -dir, and var/yok for 'there is' and 'I have'.

rules.title: The personal pronouns
rules.body: ben (I), sen (you, singular and informal), o (he, she, it), biz (we), siz (you, plural, and also polite singular), onlar (they). siz is used to one person you do not know well, as French vous. Because the endings already show the subject, the pronoun is usually dropped and stated only for emphasis or contrast.

examples.en: You are a teacher. (polite or plural)

rules.title: The 'to be' endings
rules.body: The present tense of 'to be' is a set of endings added to a noun or adjective, with four-way harmony: -im (I am), -sin (you are), no ending or -dir (he/she/it is), -iz (we are), -siniz (you are), -ler or -dirler (they are). So öğretmen gives öğretmenim, öğretmensin, öğretmen, öğretmeniz, öğretmensiniz, öğretmenler. The same set, called type I endings, is used on most verb tenses too.

rules.title: Buffer y after a vowel
rules.body: When the word ends in a vowel, the endings -im and -iz need a buffer consonant y to avoid two vowels meeting: öğrenci + -im = öğrenciyim, öğrenci + -iz = öğrenciyiz, iyi (good) gives iyiyim (I am fine). The endings -sin and -siniz begin with a consonant and need no buffer: öğrencisin, öğrencisiniz. The third person singular has no ending at all: O öğrenci.

rules.title: -dir: the optional third-person ending
rules.body: In everyday speech the third person usually has no ending: O doktor, Hava güzel. The ending -dir (-dır, -dur, -dür; -tir, -tır, -tur, -tür after a voiceless consonant) is added in formal or written statements, general truths and official notices: Ankara Türkiye'nin başkentidir. In conversation it often expresses an assumption: Ali evdedir = Ali must be at home.

examples.en: Ankara is the capital of Turkey.

rules.title: değil: 'is not'
rules.body: To negate a noun, adjective or location, put değil after it; the personal endings then attach to değil: değilim, değilsin, değil, değiliz, değilsiniz, değiller. The word itself never changes shape, so there is no harmony to worry about. değil is only for 'to be' sentences; verbs use -me- (Chapter 8) and var uses yok.

rules.title: var and yok: there is, there isn't, I have
rules.body: var means 'there is / there are' and yok 'there is not / there are not'. They come at the end of the sentence: Masada kitap var (there is a book on the table), Süt yok (there is no milk). Turkish has no verb 'to have': instead you say 'my X exists': Benim arabam var = I have a car, Zamanım yok = I have no time. Never use değil to negate var; the opposite of var is always yok.

examples.en: There is a book on the table.

rules.title: Asking 'are you...?' with mi
rules.body: A yes/no question uses the particle mi (mı, mu, mü by four-way harmony), written as a separate word after the noun or adjective; the personal ending then attaches to mi: Öğretmen misin? (Are you a teacher?), Yorgun musunuz? (Are you tired?), Türk mü? (Is he Turkish?). With var and yok: Süt var mı? Ekmek yok mu? Chapter 8 returns to questions in detail.

rules.title: Saying where you are
rules.body: A location word (a noun with the locative -de, or burada = here, orada = there) takes the personal endings directly, with buffer y after the final vowel: evdeyim (I am at home), okuldasın (you are at school), buradayız (we are here), Türkiye'deyiz. The question word nerede (where) takes the same endings: Neredesin? = Where are you?

sections.title: The present continuous -iyor and the simple present (aorist -r)
sections.summary: Turkish has two present tenses: -iyor for what is happening now (and planned events), and the aorist -r for habits, general truths, offers and promises. This chapter shows how to build both, including the negative forms, and when to use each.

rules.title: Verb stems and the infinitive -mek / -mak
rules.body: Dictionary verbs end in -mek or -mak (two-way harmony): gelmek (to come), yapmak (to do), okumak (to read). Remove that ending to get the stem, which all tenses are built on: gel-, yap-, oku-. A stem may end in a consonant (gel-, yap-) or a vowel (oku-, bekle-, başla-), and that difference affects how the present endings attach.

rules.title: The present continuous -iyor
rules.body: Add -iyor to the stem, then the personal endings: geliyorum, geliyorsun, geliyor, geliyoruz, geliyorsunuz, geliyorlar. The i of -iyor follows four-way harmony (geliyor, bakıyor, okuyor, görüyor) but the -yor part never changes. After a consonant stem the vowel is inserted: gel + iyor, yap + ıyor, gör + üyor.

rules.title: Vowel stems drop their final vowel before -iyor
rules.body: When the stem ends in a vowel, that vowel is dropped and replaced by the harmonised vowel of -iyor: başla- gives başlıyor (is starting), bekle- gives bekliyor (is waiting), oku- gives okuyor, yürü- gives yürüyor. The two-letter verbs ye- (eat) and de- (say) become yiyor and diyor. The harmony is decided by the vowel before the dropped one: başla-, so back vowel a, so -ıyor.

rules.title: Uses of -iyor and the negative -miyor
rules.body: -iyor describes what is happening now (Şimdi çalışıyorum), what is going on around now (Türkçe öğreniyorum), and planned or near-future events (Yarın İzmir'e gidiyorum = I'm going to Izmir tomorrow). The negative inserts -me-/-ma- before -iyor; the e/a is then narrowed to i/ı/u/ü by harmony: gelmiyorum (I'm not coming), yapmıyor, okumuyoruz, görmüyorlar.

examples.en: I am going to Izmir tomorrow.

rules.title: Building the aorist -r
rules.body: The aorist (geniş zaman) is the simple present. Stems ending in a vowel just add -r: başlar, yer, okur. Stems of one syllable ending in a consonant add -er/-ar: gider, yapar, bakar, içer. Stems of two or more syllables ending in a consonant add -ir/-ır/-ur/-ür: çalışır, konuşur, öğrenir, unutur. The personal endings then follow: giderim, gidersin, gider, gideriz, gidersiniz, giderler.

rules.title: Thirteen one-syllable exceptions take -ir
rules.body: A small set of common one-syllable stems take -ir/-ır/-ur/-ür instead of -er/-ar: almak (alır), bilmek (bilir), bulmak (bulur), durmak (durur), gelmek (gelir), görmek (görür), kalmak (kalır), olmak (olur), ölmek (ölür), sanmak (sanır), varmak (varır), vermek (verir), vurmak (vurur). Learn these as a list; all other one-syllable consonant stems take -er/-ar (yapar, gider, bakar, sever).

rules.title: The aorist negative: -mez, but -mem and -meyiz
rules.body: The aorist negative is irregular. Third person and second person use -mez/-maz: gelmez, gelmezsin, gelmezler, yapmaz. But the first person drops the z: gelmem (I don't come), gelmeyiz (we don't come), yapmam, yapmayız. So the full set for gelmek is gelmem, gelmezsin, gelmez, gelmeyiz, gelmezsiniz, gelmezler. Sigara içmem = I don't smoke.

rules.title: What the aorist is for
rules.body: The aorist expresses habits and routines (Her gün koşarım), general truths (Su yüz derecede kaynar), willingness and offers (Ben yaparım = I'll do it), promises (Yarın gelirim = I'll come tomorrow, I promise) and polite requests in the question form (Kapıyı açar mısın? = Would you open the door?). It is also the tense of proverbs and of 'I think so' statements: Olur (OK), Bilmem (I don't know).

rules.title: -iyor or aorist? Now versus in general
rules.body: Use -iyor for what is actually happening or currently under way, and the aorist for what happens in general. Compare Şu anda çalışıyorum (I'm working right now) with Her gün çalışırım (I work every day). Time words help: şimdi, şu anda (now) point to -iyor; her gün, her zaman, genellikle, bazen, hiç (every day, always, usually, sometimes, never) point to the aorist. Note that spoken Turkish often uses -iyor for habits too, so the aorist is the more formal or emphatic choice there.

examples.en: I sometimes go to the cinema.

sections.title: The cases and buffer letters
sections.summary: Turkish shows 'to', 'in', 'from', 'of' and the direct object with endings on the noun rather than with prepositions. This chapter introduces the five case endings, the buffer letters y and n that keep vowels apart, and the consonant changes that happen when they attach.

rules.title: Six cases, five endings
rules.body: A noun can appear in six forms. The nominative is the bare noun (ev). The other five add an ending: accusative -(y)i (the direct object), dative -(y)e (to, towards), locative -de (in, at, on), ablative -den (from, out of) and genitive -(n)in (of). The ending comes after the plural: evlerde = in the houses. On a proper noun it is separated by an apostrophe: Ankara'da, Ali'ye.

examples.target: ev, evi, eve, evde, evden, evin
examples.en: house: the house (object), to the house, in the house, from the house, of the house

rules.title: The accusative -(y)i: definite objects only
rules.body: The accusative marks a direct object, but only when it is definite, meaning a specific thing: Kitabı okuyorum = I'm reading the book. An indefinite object stays bare: Kitap okuyorum = I'm reading a book / I'm reading. The ending follows four-way harmony (-i, -ı, -u, -ü) and takes the buffer y after a vowel: arabayı, kapıyı, Ayşe'yi. Pronouns, names and nouns with 'this' or a possessive are always definite and always take it: beni, Ali'yi, bu evi.

rules.title: The dative -(y)e: to, towards, for
rules.body: The dative means 'to' or 'towards' and marks the destination or the person something is given to: eve (home, to the house), okula (to school), İstanbul'a, Ali'ye. It has two forms, -e and -a, with the buffer y after a vowel: arabaya, Ayşe'ye. The pronouns ben and sen are irregular: bana (to me), sana (to you), not 'bene', 'sene'. The dative is also used after many verbs and in prices and times: ona (to him), saat beşe (towards five).

examples.en: I bought a present for Ali.

rules.title: The locative -de / -da / -te / -ta: in, at, on
rules.body: The locative marks where something is: evde (at home), okulda (at school), masada (on the table), İstanbul'da. After a voiceless consonant (p, ç, t, k, s, ş, h, f) the d becomes t: kitapta, sokakta, Ahmet'te. With pronouns it means 'on' or 'with' a person: bende (on me, at my place), sende. There is no buffer letter; the ending simply attaches: arabada, Ayşe'de.

examples.en: The pen is on the table.
There are children in the street.
I've got the key (the key is on me).

rules.title: The ablative -den / -dan / -ten / -tan: from, out of, than
rules.body: The ablative means 'from' or 'out of': evden (from home), İstanbul'dan, okuldan. After a voiceless consonant the d becomes t: kitaptan, sokaktan, Ahmet'ten. It is used after verbs of leaving, fear and liking (korkmak, hoşlanmak, nefret etmek), for the material of something (tahtadan = made of wood), and for comparisons (Chapter 9): benden uzun = taller than me. Nereden? = Where from?

rules.title: The genitive -(n)in: of
rules.body: The genitive marks the possessor: evin (of the house), okulun, Ali'nin, Türkiye'nin. It follows four-way harmony, and after a vowel it takes the buffer n: arabanın, Ayşe'nin. The pronouns have special forms: benim (my), senin (your), onun (his, her, its), bizim (our), sizin (your), onların (their). The possessed noun then takes its own ending, which Chapter 6 covers: Ali'nin evi = Ali's house.

rules.title: Pronouns in the cases
rules.body: ben: beni, bana, bende, benden, benim. sen: seni, sana, sende, senden, senin. o: onu, ona, onda, ondan, onun (the n is part of the stem). biz: bizi, bize, bizde, bizden, bizim. siz: sizi, size, sizde, sizden, sizin. onlar: onları, onlara, onlarda, onlardan, onların. Note the irregular datives bana and sana, and the genitives benim and bizim with -im rather than -in.

rules.title: Consonant softening before a vowel ending
rules.body: Before the vowel-initial endings (accusative, dative, genitive) a final p, ç, t or k usually softens to b, c, d or ğ: kitap gives kitabı, kitaba, kitabın; ağaç gives ağacı; ekmek gives ekmeği; renk gives rengi. One-syllable words mostly do not change (at, atı; top, topu; saç, saçı), nor do many loanwords (saat, saati; millet, milleti). Proper nouns are written unchanged, Ahmet'i, even though people say 'Ahmedi'.

rules.title: Verbs that demand a particular case
rules.body: Some verbs take a different case from their English equivalents, so learn them with their case. Dative: bakmak (look at), binmek (get on), başlamak (start), sormak (ask someone), inanmak (believe), gitmek (go to). Ablative: korkmak (be afraid of), hoşlanmak (like), nefret etmek (hate), inmek (get off), çıkmak (leave). Accusative: sevmek (love), görmek (see), beklemek (wait for), aramak (look for, call).

examples.en: I am getting on the bus.

sections.title: Possession and the noun compound
sections.summary: Turkish marks the owner on the thing owned: evim is 'my house' and Ali'nin evi is 'Ali's house'. The same ending also builds everyday compounds such as Türk kahvesi (Turkish coffee). This chapter covers the possessive endings, how they combine with cases, and the difference between a genitive phrase and a compound.

rules.title: The possessive endings after a consonant
rules.body: A possessive ending on the noun says whose it is: -im (my), -in (your), -i (his, her, its), -imiz (our), -iniz (your, plural or polite), -leri (their). The vowel follows four-way harmony. So ev gives evim, evin, evi, evimiz, eviniz, evleri; okul gives okulum, okulun, okulu, okulumuz, okulunuz, okulları. These endings are different from the 'to be' endings: evim = my house, but öğretmenim = I am a teacher.

rules.title: After a vowel: -m, -n, -si, -miz, -niz, -leri
rules.body: When the noun ends in a vowel the endings lose their first vowel: araba gives arabam, araban, arabası, arabamız, arabanız, arabaları. Only the third person needs a buffer letter, and it is s, not y: arabası, annesi, Ayşe'si. Family words work the same way: annem (my mother), baban (your father), kardeşi (his or her sibling), ailemiz (our family).

rules.title: Genitive plus possessive: Ali'nin evi
rules.body: To say 'X's Y', put the genitive -(n)in on the owner and the matching possessive ending on the thing owned: Ali'nin evi (Ali's house), öğretmenin arabası (the teacher's car), Türkiye'nin başkenti (the capital of Turkey). With pronouns the genitive is optional, since the possessive ending already carries the meaning: (benim) evim, (senin) araban, (onun) kitabı. Adding the pronoun gives emphasis or contrast: Benim evim küçük, seninki büyük.

rules.title: Consonant softening and 'mine, yours'
rules.body: Because the possessive endings begin with a vowel, a final p, ç, t or k usually softens: kitabım (my book), ağacı (its tree), çocuğu (his child), köpeğimiz (our dog). To say 'mine' or 'yours' on its own, use the bare genitive pronoun: Bu kitap benim (This book is mine), O araba onların (That car is theirs). The suffix -ki builds 'the one of': benimki (mine), seninki (yours), Ayşe'ninki (Ayşe's one).

rules.title: Case endings after a possessive: the buffer n
rules.body: A case ending can follow a possessive ending: evimde (in my house), evimden, evime. After the third-person possessive -(s)i, every case ending needs a buffer n: evine (to his house), evinde (in his house), evinden, evinin, and the accusative becomes -ni: evini (his house, as object), arabasını. So evi can mean 'his house' or 'the house (object)', but 'his house (object)' is unambiguously evini.

examples.en: I am going to Ali's house.
He / she is selling his / her car.
He / she got a letter from his / her mother.

rules.title: The noun compound: Türk kahvesi
rules.body: Two nouns can form a compound where the first noun describes the type of the second: the second noun takes the third-person possessive -(s)i and the first noun stays bare. Türk kahvesi (Turkish coffee), çay bardağı (tea glass), otobüs durağı (bus stop), yatak odası (bedroom), İngiliz anahtarı (adjustable spanner, literally English key). Most everyday compound words in Turkish are built this way, including many place names: Taksim Meydanı, Kadıköy İskelesi.

rules.title: Compound or genitive phrase?
rules.body: The genitive phrase names a specific owner; the compound names a kind. Ali'nin kahvesi is Ali's coffee, the cup belonging to Ali; Türk kahvesi is Turkish coffee, a type of drink. Okulun kapısı is the door of a particular school; okul kapısı is a school door, a kind of door. The test is the first noun: genitive -(n)in means a specific possessor, bare noun means a category.

rules.title: Having things: possessive plus var / yok
rules.body: Since Turkish has no verb 'to have', possession is 'my X exists': Arabam var (I have a car), Kardeşin var mı? (Do you have a sibling?), Vaktim yok (I have no time). The owner may be named with the genitive for emphasis: Benim iki kardeşim var. In the past, use vardı and yoktu: Param yoktu (I had no money).

examples.en: Do you have any brothers or sisters?

rules.title: Plural and possessive together
rules.body: The order of endings is fixed: noun, plural, possessive, case. arkadaşlarım (my friends), arkadaşlarımdan (from my friends), evlerimizde (in our houses). The third person plural is ambiguous: evleri can mean 'their house', 'his houses' or 'their houses', and context decides. Note that -leri is used once, never doubled: 'their houses' is evleri, not 'evlerleri'.

sections.title: Past tenses: -di and -miş
sections.summary: Turkish has two simple pasts. -di reports what you know for certain, usually because you saw it; -miş reports what you were told, inferred or only just noticed. This chapter builds both, including the past of 'to be', negatives and questions.

rules.title: The definite past -di
rules.body: Add -di (-dı, -du, -dü) to the stem, then the past-tense personal endings, called type II: -m, -n, no ending, -k, -niz, -ler. gelmek gives geldim, geldin, geldi, geldik, geldiniz, geldiler. The vowel of -di follows four-way harmony: geldi, aldı, okudu, gördü. This tense is used for completed events the speaker knows for sure, and corresponds to both English 'I came' and 'I have come'.

examples.en: We went to the cinema yesterday.

rules.title: -ti after a voiceless consonant
rules.body: After p, ç, t, k, s, ş, h or f the d of -di becomes t: yaptım (I did), içtik (we drank), baktı (he looked), koştu (he ran), gittim (I went). Notice that the t of git- does not soften here because the suffix begins with a consonant. The type II endings never change this: yaptım, yaptın, yaptı, yaptık, yaptınız, yaptılar.

rules.title: Negative and question in the -di past
rules.body: The negative inserts -me-/-ma- before -di: gelmedim, gelmedin, gelmedi, gelmedik, gelmediniz, gelmediler; yapmadım, görmedik. The question particle mi follows the complete verb, including the personal ending: Geldin mi? (Did you come?), Gördünüz mü? (Did you see?), Anlamadın mı? (Didn't you understand?). This differs from the present tenses, where the ending moves onto mi.

rules.title: The past of 'to be': -(y)di
rules.body: A noun, adjective or location takes -(y)di plus the type II endings: yorgundum (I was tired), öğretmendi (he was a teacher), evdeydim (I was at home), hastaydı (she was ill). After a vowel the buffer y appears: hastaydım, buradaydık. After a voiceless consonant it is -ti: Türktü, açtık (we were hungry). The negative is değildi: Yorgun değildim. var and yok become vardı and yoktu.

rules.title: The reported past -miş
rules.body: Add -miş (-mış, -muş, -müş) to the stem, then the type I endings: gelmişim, gelmişsin, gelmiş, gelmişiz, gelmişsiniz, gelmişler. Use -miş for events you did not witness yourself: something you were told (Ali gelmiş = I hear Ali has come), something you infer from evidence (Yağmur yağmış = it must have rained, the ground is wet), or something you only just discovered, often with surprise (Çok güzel olmuş! = it's turned out great!).

examples.en: It has turned out really nice!
I seem to have fallen asleep.

rules.title: -miş with 'to be', var and değil
rules.body: The reported past also attaches to nouns and adjectives: hastaymış (apparently he is or was ill), öğretmenmiş, yokmuş, varmış, değilmiş. Fairy tales begin Bir varmış, bir yokmuş (once upon a time, literally 'there was one, there wasn't one'). The negative verb takes -miş after -me-: gelmemiş (apparently he didn't come). In questions the personal ending moves onto mi, as in the present tenses: Gelmiş mi? Gelmiş misin? Duymuş musunuz? (Have you heard?)

examples.en: There is no bread, I'm told.

rules.title: -di or -miş? Witnessed or not
rules.body: Choose -di when you know the event directly: you saw it, did it or are stating it as a fact. Choose -miş when the knowledge is second-hand or inferred. Ali geldi: I saw him arrive. Ali gelmiş: someone told me, or I see his coat on the hook. Talking about your own past, -miş implies you were not aware at the time: Uyumuşum (I must have slept). News reports and history use -di for facts and -miş for what sources claim.

examples.en: Ali came (I know, I saw him).

rules.title: Time words and the past continuous -iyordu
rules.body: Common past time words: dün (yesterday), dün akşam (last night), geçen hafta (last week), geçen yıl (last year), önce after a period means 'ago': iki yıl önce (two years ago). To say what was going on at a moment, put -di on the -iyor form: çalışıyordum (I was working), uyuyordu (he was sleeping). Sen aradığında uyuyordum = I was sleeping when you called.

sections.title: Questions and negation
sections.summary: Turkish asks yes/no questions with the little particle mi and negates verbs with -me-, nouns with değil and existence with yok. This chapter pulls those threads together: where mi goes and what it focuses on, the question words, and the negative words that must pair with a negative verb.

rules.title: The particle mi
rules.body: A yes/no question adds mi (mı, mu, mü by four-way harmony) after the word being asked about. It is written as a separate word but harmonises with the word before it. In the present tenses and with 'to be' the personal ending attaches to mi: Geliyor musun? (Are you coming?), Öğretmen misiniz? (Are you a teacher?), Türk mü? In the -di past the ending stays on the verb: Geldin mi? (Did you come?).

rules.title: Moving mi to change the focus
rules.body: mi normally follows the verb, which questions the whole sentence. Placed after another word, it questions that word alone. Ali bugün okula gidiyor mu? asks whether Ali is going. Ali bugün okula mı gidiyor? asks whether it is school he is going to. Ali bugün mü okula gidiyor? asks whether it is today. Ali mi bugün okula gidiyor? asks whether it is Ali. The verb then keeps its own personal ending.

examples.en: Is it school that Ali is going to?
Is it today that you're going?

rules.title: Question words
rules.body: ne (what), kim (who), nerede (where), nereye (where to), nereden (where from), ne zaman (when), nasıl (how), neden / niçin / niye (why), kaç (how many), ne kadar (how much), hangi (which). They are never used together with mi. The question word stands where the answer would stand, usually just before the verb, and the word order otherwise stays the same: Nerede oturuyorsun? Kim geldi? Saat kaç? (What time is it?).

rules.title: Negating a verb with -me-
rules.body: The negative suffix -me-/-ma- goes directly after the stem, before any tense ending: gelmiyorum (I'm not coming), gelmedim (I didn't come), gelmem / gelmez (I don't / he doesn't come), gelmemiş (apparently he didn't come), gelmeyeceğim (I won't come). Before -iyor the vowel narrows to i/ı/u/ü (gelmiyor, bakmıyor), and before -ecek the buffer y appears (gelmeyecek). The imperative is simply gelme! (don't come).

rules.title: değil for nouns, adjectives and contrast
rules.body: değil negates 'to be' sentences: Yorgun değilim (I'm not tired), Bu kolay değil. It also negates a single word to set up a contrast, with the correction following: Ali değil, Ayşe geldi (It wasn't Ali who came, it was Ayşe). Bugün değil, yarın (not today, tomorrow). It is not used to negate verbs: 'geliyor değilim' is not the normal way to say 'I'm not coming'.

rules.title: yok, hayır and evet
rules.body: yok is the negative of var: Ekmek var mı? Yok. (Is there bread? There isn't.) In speech yok also serves as a casual 'no' and hayır is the standard 'no'; evet is 'yes'. Turks often answer a yes/no question by repeating the verb rather than with a bare yes or no: Geldin mi? Geldim. / Gelmedim. Çay içer misin? İçerim. (Yes, I'd love one.)

examples.en: Is there bread? No, there isn't.
Would you like tea? Yes, please.

rules.title: Negative questions and the tag değil mi?
rules.body: A negative verb takes mi like any other: Gelmiyor musun? (Aren't you coming?), Anlamadın mı? (Didn't you understand?). The tag question değil mi? (isn't it? don't you? etc.) is added, unchanged, to any statement: Hava güzel, değil mi? Türkçe öğreniyorsun, değil mi? It is the all-purpose equivalent of every English tag question.

examples.en: The weather is nice, isn't it?

rules.title: hiç, kimse and hiçbir: double negatives are required
rules.body: Words like hiç (ever, at all), kimse (anybody, nobody), hiçbir şey (anything, nothing), hiçbir zaman / asla (never) and hiçbir yer (anywhere, nowhere) must be used with a negative verb or with yok. Kimse gelmedi (nobody came), Hiçbir şey görmedim (I saw nothing), Hiç kimse yok (there's nobody). Unlike English, this doubling is correct and compulsory. In a question, hiç means 'ever': Hiç İstanbul'a gittin mi?

examples.en: Have you ever been to Istanbul?

exercises.explain: The last vowel e gives mi: Öğretmen mi?
After ü the particle is mü: Türk mü?
mu after u, with the ending -sun attached.

exercises.explain: mu after -yor, with -sunuz attached.

exercises.explain: It harmonises with the preceding word but is spelled separately: Geliyor musun?
A question word replaces mi and stands before the verb; nerede = where (at).

exercises.explain: A question word makes the sentence a question by itself; mi is not added.

exercises.q: Sen ___ geldin? (When did you come? two words)
exercises.explain: ne zaman means 'when' and goes before the verb.

exercises.q: Which is correct for 'Did you come?'
exercises.explain: In the -di past the ending stays on the verb; the ending moves onto mi only in the present tenses.

exercises.q: 'Ali bugün okula mı gidiyor?' asks specifically about ...
exercises.explain: mi follows okula, so the question is whether it is school he is going to.

exercises.q: Bugün ___. (I'm not working today; çalışmak, present continuous)
exercises.explain: The negative -ma- narrows to -mı- before -yor.

options: right after the stem, before the tense ending
at the start of the verb
exercises.explain: gel-me-di-m: stem, negative, tense, person.

exercises.explain: değil negates a single word to set up a contrast.
var takes the particle mı by harmony; the particle normally follows var.
In casual speech yok is also used for 'no'.

exercises.q: Hava güzel, ___ mi? (The weather is nice, isn't it?)
exercises.explain: değil mi? is the universal tag question.
Negative -mi- plus the question particle gives a negative question.

exercises.q: In 'Hiç kimse gelmedi' (Nobody came) the verb must be negative.
exercises.explain: kimse and hiç require a negative verb; the double negative is compulsory.

exercises.q: ___ kimse yok. (There is nobody at all; the word meaning 'at all')
exercises.explain: hiç strengthens the negative: hiç kimse = nobody at all.

exercises.q: Which answer to 'Çay içer misin?' means 'Yes, I'd love one'?
exercises.explain: Turks answer by repeating the verb: içerim = I'll drink (one).

exercises.q: Sen ___ gidiyorsun? (Where are you going? nere + dative)
exercises.explain: nereye = to where; nerede would ask where you are.
değil + mi turns the negative statement into a question.

exercises.q: 'değil' is the normal way to negate a verb: 'geliyor değilim' = 'I'm not coming'.
exercises.explain: Verbs are negated with -me-: gelmiyorum.
Literally 'hour how many', the standard way to ask the time.
The last vowel of İngiliz is i, so the particle is mi with no ending for the third person.

sections.title: Adjectives, comparison and postpositions
sections.summary: Turkish adjectives never change form, comparison uses daha and en with the ablative, and the work of English prepositions is done by postpositions that follow the noun, some of which demand a particular case. This chapter covers all three.

rules.title: Adjectives: before the noun, never changing
rules.body: An adjective stands before its noun and takes no ending for number or case: güzel ev, güzel evler, güzel evlerde. As a predicate it comes at the end with the 'to be' endings: Ev güzel (the house is nice), Yorgunum (I am tired). Many adjectives also work as nouns: genç (young; a young person), yaşlı (old; an old person), hasta (ill; a patient).

examples.en: The young people are in the park.

rules.title: Comparative: ablative plus daha
rules.body: To compare, put the ablative -den on the thing compared with and daha (more) before the adjective: Ali Ayşe'den daha uzun (Ali is taller than Ayşe). When the ablative is present, daha can be dropped: Ali Ayşe'den uzun. Without a point of comparison, daha alone means 'more / -er': Bu daha güzel (this is nicer). 'Less' is daha az: daha az pahalı (less expensive).

examples.en: The bus is cheaper than a taxi.

rules.title: Superlative: en
rules.body: en before the adjective gives the superlative: en büyük (the biggest), en güzel şehir (the most beautiful city). The group is shown with a genitive phrase or a locative: Türkiye'nin en büyük şehri (Turkey's biggest city), sınıfta en çalışkan öğrenci (the hardest-working student in the class). 'Than anyone / anything' uses herkesten / her şeyden with daha: herkesten daha hızlı (faster than everyone).

examples.en: The hardest-working student in the class is Ayşe.

rules.title: kadar and gibi: as ... as, like
rules.body: kadar after a bare noun means 'as ... as': Ali Ayşe kadar uzun (Ali is as tall as Ayşe), senin kadar (as much as you). gibi means 'like': kuş gibi (like a bird), benim gibi (like me). Pronouns take the genitive before both: benim kadar, senin gibi, onun gibi. Note that o, bu, şu also take the genitive: onun gibi, bunun gibi.

examples.en: Ali is as tall as Ayşe.
You're not as tired as me.

rules.title: Intensifiers and doubled adjectives
rules.body: çok (very), biraz (a bit), pek (quite, in negatives: not very), fazla (too), o kadar (so) go before the adjective: çok güzel, biraz pahalı, pek iyi değil, fazla sıcak. Colours and some adjectives can be intensified by doubling the first syllable with an inserted consonant: bembeyaz (snow white), kapkara (pitch black), yemyeşil (bright green), sımsıcak (piping hot), upuzun (very long). These forms are fixed and must be learned individually.

rules.title: Postpositions after a bare noun: için, ile, gibi, kadar
rules.body: Turkish uses postpositions, which come after the noun. için (for), ile (with, by), gibi (like) and kadar (as ... as) follow a bare noun: Ali için (for Ali), araba ile (by car), kuş gibi. Personal pronouns and demonstratives take the genitive before them: benim için (for me), seninle (with you), onun gibi (like him), bunun için (for this reason). Exception: onlar stays bare before ile and gibi (onlarla, onlar gibi).

rules.title: ile as a suffix: -(y)le / -(y)la
rules.body: ile is usually attached to the noun as -le/-la, with the buffer y after a vowel: otobüsle (by bus), arabayla (by car), Ali'yle (with Ali), annemle (with my mother). The pronouns give benimle, seninle, onunla, bizimle, sizinle, onlarla. The suffixed form is the normal one in speech; the separate word ile is slightly more formal and also means 'and' in lists: çay ile kahve.

examples.en: We went to the cinema with Ali.

rules.title: Postpositions with the ablative: sonra, önce, başka, beri
rules.body: sonra (after), önce (before), başka (other than), beri (since) and dolayı (because of) require the ablative on the noun before them: okuldan sonra (after school), yemekten önce (before the meal), senden başka (apart from you), sabahtan beri (since morning). After a length of time, sonra and önce take no ablative and mean 'later' and 'ago': iki saat sonra (two hours later), iki yıl önce (two years ago).

examples.en: After school we go to the park.
Wash your hands before the meal.

rules.title: Postpositions with the dative: kadar, doğru, göre, karşı
rules.body: A second group takes the dative: kadar meaning 'until, as far as' (akşama kadar = until evening, İzmir'e kadar = as far as Izmir), doğru (towards: eve doğru), göre (according to: bana göre = in my opinion), karşı (against, facing: duvara karşı), rağmen (despite: yağmura rağmen). Note that kadar changes meaning with the case: Ali kadar (as much as Ali) but Ali'ye kadar (up to Ali).

examples.en: In my opinion this is right.

exercises.explain: Adjective, then bir, then the singular noun.
The point of comparison takes the ablative: benden = than me.

exercises.q: Ali ___ daha uzun. (Ali is taller than Ayşe; Ayşe + ablative)
exercises.explain: Ayşe'den daha uzun: ablative on the name, apostrophe included.

exercises.q: İstanbul Türkiye'nin ___ büyük şehri. (Istanbul is Turkey's biggest city; superlative word)
exercises.explain: en before the adjective makes the superlative.

exercises.q: Turkish adjectives agree with the noun in number: 'güzeller evler'.
exercises.explain: Adjectives never change: güzel evler.

exercises.q: 'Ali is as tall as Ayşe' is ...
exercises.explain: kadar after a bare noun means 'as ... as'.

exercises.q: Bu senin ___. (This is for you; postposition)
exercises.explain: için = for; a pronoun before it takes the genitive: senin için.
Pronouns take the genitive before ile: benim + le.

exercises.q: ___ sonra parka gidiyoruz. (After school we go to the park; okul + ablative)
exercises.explain: sonra requires the ablative: okuldan sonra.

exercises.q: 'sonra' and 'önce' take the ablative on the noun before them.
exercises.explain: yemekten önce, okuldan sonra.

exercises.en: Wash your hands before the meal.

exercises.q: 'in my opinion / according to me' is ...
exercises.explain: göre takes the dative: bana göre.

exercises.q: ___ kadar çalıştım. (I worked until evening; akşam + dative)
exercises.explain: kadar meaning 'until' takes the dative.
gibi = like.

exercises.q: Nouns take the genitive before 'gibi' and 'için': 'evin için'.
exercises.explain: Nouns stay bare (ev için); only pronouns and demonstratives take the genitive.

exercises.q: ___ sinemaya gittim. (I went to the cinema with Ali; Ali + ile as a suffix)
exercises.explain: ile attaches as -yle after a vowel, with an apostrophe on the name.
Doubling the first syllable intensifies the adjective.

exercises.en: Ayşe is the hardest-working student in the class.

exercises.q: Bu kitap o kitaptan ___ ilginç. (This book is more interesting than that book)
exercises.explain: daha = more; the ablative marks the thing compared.
herkes + ten (than everyone) + daha hızlı (faster).

exercises.q: 'Ali Ayşe'den uzun.' without 'daha' is also correct Turkish.
exercises.explain: When the ablative is present, daha is optional.
-le is the suffixed form of ile: with / by bus.

exercises.q: İki saat ___ geldi. (He came two hours ago)
exercises.explain: After a length of time, önce means 'ago' and takes no ablative.
daha alone before an adjective gives the comparative.

exercises.q: Pronouns take the genitive before 'ile', 'için' and 'gibi': 'benim için', 'senin gibi'.
exercises.explain: benim için, seninle, onun gibi; only onlar stays bare before ile and gibi.

exercises.q: ___ doğru yürüdük. (We walked towards the house; ev + dative)
exercises.explain: doğru (towards) takes the dative.

sections.title: Future, ability and polite requests
sections.summary: This chapter adds the future tense -ecek, the ability suffix -ebil and the polite request form -ebilir misiniz?, and finishes with the numbers and how to tell the time, which together let you make plans, ask for help and arrange to meet.

rules.title: The future -(y)ecek / -(y)acak
rules.body: Add -ecek/-acak to the stem and then the type I endings. The final k softens to ğ before a vowel ending: geleceğim, geleceksin, gelecek, geleceğiz, geleceksiniz, gelecekler; yapacağım, yapacaksın, yapacak. After a vowel stem the buffer y appears: okuyacak, bekleyecek, başlayacağım. The verbs ye- and de- become yiyecek and diyecek. The future is used for predictions, decisions and promises: Yarın yağmur yağacak.

rules.title: Future negative and question
rules.body: The negative inserts -me-/-ma- with the buffer y before -ecek: gelmeyeceğim (I won't come), yapmayacak (he won't do it), gitmeyeceğiz. The question particle takes the personal ending: Gelecek misin? (Will you come?), Yapacak mısınız? Note the difference from the aorist question Gelir misin?, which is a request ('would you come?') rather than a question about the future.

rules.title: Ability: -(y)ebil + aorist
rules.body: 'Can' is the suffix -ebil/-abil added to the stem, after which the verb is conjugated normally, most often in the aorist: gelebilirim (I can come), yapabilirsin, okuyabilir (buffer y after a vowel), görebiliriz. It also combines with other tenses: gelebildim (I was able to come), gelebileceğim (I'll be able to come). The negative does not use -bil at all: it is -eme/-ama with the aorist negative: gelemem (I can't come), yapamaz, gelemiyorum (I can't come right now), gelemedim (I couldn't come).

rules.title: Possibility and permission with -ebilir
rules.body: In the third person -ebilir also expresses possibility: Yarın yağmur yağabilir (it may rain tomorrow), Ali gelmeyebilir (Ali might not come; here -me- comes before -yebil). With 'I' and 'we' as a question it asks permission: Girebilir miyim? (May I come in?), Oturabilir miyiz? (May we sit here?). This form is already polite on its own, so lütfen is optional.

rules.title: Polite requests: -ebilir misiniz? and lütfen
rules.body: The politest everyday request is the ability question in the aorist, addressed as siz: Yardım edebilir misiniz? (Could you help?), Kapıyı kapatabilir misiniz? To a friend use misin: Tuzu uzatabilir misin? Slightly less formal is the plain aorist question: Kapıyı açar mısınız? The imperative plus lütfen is direct but polite with the -in/-iniz ending: Lütfen oturun (please sit down), Buyurun (here you are / please go ahead). Teşekkür ederim is 'thank you', rica ederim 'you're welcome'.

rules.title: Numbers
rules.body: 1 bir, 2 iki, 3 üç, 4 dört, 5 beş, 6 altı, 7 yedi, 8 sekiz, 9 dokuz, 10 on; 20 yirmi, 30 otuz, 40 kırk, 50 elli, 60 altmış, 70 yetmiş, 80 seksen, 90 doksan, 100 yüz, 1000 bin. Larger numbers are built by simple juxtaposition: on bir (11), yirmi beş (25), iki yüz (200), bin iki yüz elli (1250). 'One hundred' and 'one thousand' are just yüz and bin, without bir. Ordinals add -inci: birinci (first), ikinci, üçüncü, dördüncü, beşinci.

rules.title: Telling the time
rules.body: Saat kaç? asks the time. On the hour: Saat üç (it's three). Half past: Saat üç buçuk. Past the hour, the hour takes the accusative and geçiyor follows: Üçü on geçiyor (ten past three), Üçü çeyrek geçiyor (quarter past three). To the hour, the hour takes the dative and var follows: Üçe on var (ten to three), Üçe çeyrek var (quarter to three). Minutes are simply numbers: dokuzu yirmi beş geçiyor (9:25).

examples.en: What time is it? It's five.

rules.title: Saying 'at' a time, and ages
rules.body: 'At' an hour uses the locative: saat üçte (at three), üç buçukta (at half past three), saat kaçta? (at what time?). For 'at ten past' and 'at ten to', the forms change to geçe and kala: üçü on geçe (at ten past three), üçe on kala (at ten to three). Ages use yaş with the locative and 'to be' endings: Kaç yaşındasın? (How old are you?), Yirmi beş yaşındayım (I'm twenty-five).

examples.en: Let's meet at ten past three.

rules.title: Future time expressions
rules.body: yarın (tomorrow), öbür gün (the day after tomorrow), gelecek hafta or haftaya (next week), gelecek ay (next month), gelecek yıl / seneye (next year), bu akşam (tonight), birazdan (in a moment). After a length of time, sonra means 'in / later': iki saat sonra (in two hours). The days: Pazartesi, Salı, Çarşamba, Perşembe, Cuma, Cumartesi, Pazar; 'on Monday' is simply Pazartesi or Pazartesi günü, with no case ending.

examples.en: Next week we will go to Istanbul.
I'll be there in two hours.

exercises.explain: gel-ecek-im, with k softening to ğ before the vowel.

exercises.q: The future of 'yapmak' (to do), third person, is ...
exercises.explain: After the back vowel a the suffix is -acak; yapıcak is only a colloquial pronunciation.

exercises.q: Yarın okula ___. (I will go to school tomorrow; gitmek)
exercises.explain: git- softens to gid- before the vowel of -ecek, and k becomes ğ before -im.

exercises.q: Biz yarın ___. (We will come tomorrow; gelmek)
exercises.explain: gel-ecek-iz, with ğ before the vowel ending.

exercises.q: In 'geleceğim' the k of -ecek softens to ğ before the vowel of -im.
exercises.explain: k softens to ğ whenever a vowel-initial ending follows: geleceğim, geleceğiz.

exercises.q: 'okumak' (to read) in the future, third person, is ...
exercises.explain: A vowel stem takes the buffer y: oku-y-acak.

exercises.q: Bugün ___. (I won't work today; çalışmak, future negative)
exercises.explain: çalış-ma-y-acak-ım, with buffer y and k softening to ğ.
The personal ending attaches to mi; Gelir misin? is a request, not a prediction.

exercises.en: Next week we will go to Istanbul.

exercises.explain: gel-ebil-ir-im: ability suffix, aorist, first person.

exercises.q: Türkçe ___. (I can speak Turkish; konuşmak + ability, aorist)
exercises.explain: konuş-abil-ir-im.

exercises.q: The negative of 'gelebilirim' (I can come) is 'gelebilmem'.
exercises.explain: The negative of ability drops -bil-: gelemem (I can't come).
-eme- plus the aorist negative: gelemem; gelemiyorum is also used in speech.

exercises.q: The polite 'Could you help me?' is ...
exercises.explain: -ebilir misiniz? is the standard polite request form.
mi plus the first-person ending with buffer y: miyim.
Third-person -ebilir expresses possibility.

exercises.q: 'Lütfen oturun.' is a polite way of saying 'Please sit down'.
exercises.explain: The -un imperative is the polite or plural form; lütfen adds 'please'.
Tens then units, simply placed side by side.
kırk = forty; the tens are not built from the units in Turkish.
yüz = hundred, bin = thousand; no bir is needed.

exercises.q: Saat ___? (What time is it? the word for 'how many')
exercises.explain: Saat kaç? literally asks 'hour how many?'
buçuk = half, so üç buçuk is half past three.
Dative plus var counts towards the hour: a quarter to three.

exercises.q: 'Üçü on geçiyor.' means 'It's ten past three'.
exercises.explain: Accusative plus geçiyor counts past the hour.

exercises.q: Toplantı saat ___ başlıyor. (The meeting starts at five; beş + locative)
exercises.explain: 'At' an hour is the locative; after ş the ending is -te.
-inci makes ordinals: ikinci = second.

exercises.q: Yarın yağmur ___. (It will rain tomorrow; yağmak, future)
exercises.explain: yağ-acak: third person has no personal ending.
